title: Cells Go Around, Exit Sets the Stay

scenes.tts: Drain the thoracic duct of a rat for a few days, and the lymph runs short of lymphocytes. The usual view was that lymph nodes made those cells. If so, and they were released once, output should hold roughly steady. If the same cells go around a loop, removing them should empty it.

scenes.tts: Gowans left a cannula, a fine tube, in the thoracic duct of rats and collected lymph for days. Output fell progressively. When he returned the collected cells by vein, output recovered, and the returned cells turned up again in duct lymph. The cells were going around: from blood, through lymphoid tissue, into lymph, and back to blood.

scenes.tts: Labelled lymphocytes injected by vein into rats moved quickly into nodes, across the walls of high endothelial venules. A node has two entrances, afferent lymph and these venules, and one exit, the efferent lymphatic. In large animals at rest, more than ninety percent of lymphocytes in efferent lymph came in through the venules. L selectin tethers the cell, and it rolls. A chemokine signal switches the integrin L F A one, which grips I C A M one and two. The cell stops, then crosses.
scenes.visual: node block with two entrances and one exit, share bar; then venule wall close-up: tether, roll, chemokine, LFA-1 switch, grip, cross

scenes.tts: Getting out needs a receptor. The lipid sphingosine one phosphate is high in blood and lymph, and low inside lymphoid tissue. Lymphocytes carry a receptor for it, S one P one. In mice whose blood-forming cells lacked it, mature T cells could not leave the thymus. Deficient T and B cells transferred into normal mice could not leave lymphoid organs. So the need lies in the lymphocyte itself.

scenes.tts: Exit sets how long a cell stays. The mean residence time is one divided by the exit rate constant. In a fitted rat model, the spleen's exit rate constant is zero point zero zero seven per minute. That gives about two point four hours. A subcutaneous node holds a cell about ten hours, and blood about twenty-six seconds per pass. At steady state, relative to blood, the spleen holds eight times as many cells, the subcutaneous nodes about fifteen. This keeps only those three; lung, liver and cell loss are left out.
scenes.visual: equation, spleen worked example, bars of cells held relative to blood with residence times
scenes.caption: Exit sets how long a cell stays. The mean residence time is 1 divided by the exit rate constant. In a fitted rat model, the spleen's exit rate constant is 0.007 per minute. That gives about 2.4 hours. A subcutaneous node holds a cell about 10 hours, and blood about 26 seconds per pass. At steady state, relative to blood, the spleen holds 8 times as many cells, the subcutaneous nodes about 15. This keeps only those three; lung, liver and cell loss are left out.

scenes.tts: A node that drains a site of immune challenge changes its traffic. In mouse studies, its lymphocytes express C D sixty-nine, which removes S one P one. Entry from blood continues, but exit slows. If entry is unchanged and the exit rate constant halves, residence time doubles, and so does the number held. The shutdown is transient. Keep this: at steady state, cells held equal entry times residence.
scenes.visual: CD69 strips S1P1, exit arrow thins, cells held doubles; exit resumes; rule
